newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House panel seeks retribution for CRP mishap.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House panel seeks retribution for CRP mishap.

text.p: The House Appropriations Committee on Wednesday voted 28-21 to fire two mid-level USDA officials in response to what one member described as the mishandling of the Conservation Reserve Program signup in Washington state this past spring.
The panel took the action as part of a nearly $50 billion spending bill to fund U.S. Agriculture Department and Food and Drug Adminstration programs in fiscal 1998.

However, Wisconsin Rep. David Obey, the top Democrat on the appropriations panel, voted against the overall spending package because of the CRP amendment and several other provisions approved by the Republican-controlled panel.
Ohio Rep. Marcy Kaptur, the top Democrat on the appropriations subcommittee on agiculture, also voted against the bill, as did most Democrats.

Rep. George Nethercutt, a Washington Republican, offered the amendment to eliminate the positions held by Farm Service Agency Deputy Administrator Richard Newman and Assistant Deputy Adminstrator Parks Shackleford.

Washington farmers this past spring offered to enroll 819,378 acres into the CRP, which pays farmers an annual rental payment to keep land out of production. But to the great surprise of local officials, USDA only accepted 172,013 acres, or about 20 percent, of the acres offered in Washington.
Meanwhile, USDA accepted nearly 80 percent of the land offered in neighboring Idaho and Oregon.
Originally, Nethercutt set his sights on firing Lynn Brown, USDA's top Natural Resource Conservation Service official in Washington state.

He offered an amendment to do that three weeks ago when the agriculture appropriation subcommittee met on the fiscal 1998 spending bill, but he withdrew it at the request of the subcommittee chairman.

Nethercutt told reporters Wednesday that he changed his mind about who to blame after learning that Washington NRSC officials had submitted a plan for rectifying the low signup results that was rejected by Newman and Shackleford.
As the result of the "imcompetence" of those two officials, "my farmers suffered a great loss," Nethercutt said.

USDA officials up to Secretary Dan Glickman have ruled out reopening last spring's enrollment or reevaluating Washington's bids. However, they have said they will considering broadening air quality criteria for the next signup later this year to take into account Washington's volcanic soils.
"We believe we've done our best," USDA Spokesman Tom Amontree told Reuters. "While we understand (Nethercutt's) frustration, we feel it's unfortunate that he would express it in such a personal way."
The fiscal 1998 spending will move to the House floor and then to the Senate in the coming weeks, where the provision eliminating the two USDA jobs could be dropped or modified.
"We've been working with the congressman and the Washington delegation on their concerns," Amontree said. "It would be very unfortunate" if the provision is part of the final bill.
Rep. John Porter of Illinois was the only Republican on the appropriations panel to vote against Nethercutt's amendment. No Democrat voted for the measure.
Top Democrat Obey said approval of the amendment would bring shame on the committee. "I think, with all due respect, that's using our position in a bullying way," he said.
